question: Pre-Reading Q1: The title of the text is 'The Role of Women in Pakistan's Creation and Development'. What do you think the lesson will be about?
answer: The title tells us that the lesson will be about the part played by women in the making of Pakistan and in its progress afterwards. I think it will describe women who worked shoulder to shoulder with men during the freedom movement, and also women who have served the country in education, health, social welfare and other fields since 1947. It will probably show that Pakistan could neither have been created nor developed without the sacrifices and services of its daughters.
explanation: This is a prediction task: the students must use the title and key words to guess the content of the text before reading it. Predicting from the title prepares the mind for the topic and makes reading faster and more meaningful.

question: Pre-Reading Q2: Can you think of names of some famous women in Pakistan's history?
answer: Yes. Mohtarma Fatima Jinnah (Madr-e-Millat), Begum Ra'ana Liaquat Ali Khan, Begum Jahan Ara Shahnawaz, Lady Sughra Hidayatullah, Lady Nusrat Haroon, Begum Shaista Ikramullah, Begum Salma Tassaduque Hussain, Bi Amman, Begum Mahmooda Salim Khan and Fatima Begum are some of the famous women of Pakistan's history. They are remembered for their services to the freedom movement and to the new country.
explanation: This pre-reading question activates the students' prior knowledge of history. Naming famous women of the past helps them connect the new text with what they already know.

question: Pre-Reading Q3: Can you think of some names of women who have recently achieved fame in Pakistan?

question: Exercise 2 (Vocabulary): Work in pairs, find the following words in the text and underline them: opinions, access, contribution, philanthropist, tireless, simultaneously, renowned, inspired, recognition, rehearsed, enthusiasm. Then try to guess the meanings of these words and check them from the glossary.
answer:
Meanings of the given words as they are used in the text:
1. opinions - the views or beliefs that a person holds about something.
2. access - the right or opportunity to use, approach or obtain something.
3. contribution - something that a person gives to help achieve or supply something.
4. philanthropist - a rich person who generously helps others, especially by giving money to good causes.
5. tireless - working without becoming tired; full of continuous energy and effort.
6. simultaneously - at the same time.
7. renowned - famous and admired for a special quality or skill.
8. inspired - filled with the desire and confidence to do something, usually after seeing somebody else's good example.
9. recognition - the appreciation or honour shown to a person for what he or she has done; the act of knowing somebody or something again.
10. rehearsed - practised a speech, play or performance before presenting it in public.
11. enthusiasm - a strong feeling of eager interest and excitement.
explanation: These words are taken directly from the reading text. Guessing their meaning from the surrounding sentences, and then checking in the glossary, trains the students to use context clues instead of memorising words.

question: Exercise 9: Work in groups of three. Think of one thing that you can do during the summer vacations that will help people or improve things in the area where you live. Use the IDEAL tool to identify the problem and find the solution (Identify, Define, Explore, Action, Look back). Next decide: who will do what, what things you will need, by what time you will do the different things, and when you will complete the task. Then share your plan with the class.
answer:
Model group plan (groups of three): 'Turn a rubbish corner of our street into a small green reading corner for children.'

IDENTIFY - What is the problem we want to address? The open corner of our street is used as a dumping place for garbage. It is dirty and smelly, mosquitoes breed there, and the small children of the street have no clean, safe place to sit and read or play during the summer holidays.

DEFINE - What do we want to do? We want to clean that corner, plant a few shady plants in pots and set up a small 'summer reading and games corner' where the young children of the street can spend two hours every afternoon.

EXPLORE - Find details about the problem. We visited the corner and counted how much rubbish was there. We found out that the municipal office will give two dustbins free of cost if we apply in writing. We asked the neighbours and they promised to give old story books, board games and a mat. We also asked the children what they would like.

ACTION - What steps will we take to address the problem?
(1) Hold a clean-up day and clear all the rubbish.
(2) Write an application to the municipal office for two dustbins.
(3) Collect story books, games, a mat and two benches from the neighbours.
(4) Plant four small shady plants in pots.
(5) Fix a duty rota so that two of us look after the corner every afternoon.

LOOK BACK - How will we check that we have done our task? At the end of the vacation we will see whether the corner is still clean, count how many children used it every day, and ask the neighbours and the children for their opinion. If the plan has worked, we will request the school to continue it.

Next, decide:
- Who will do what: Sana will lead the clean-up and write to the municipal office; Bilal will collect the books, games and benches; Ayesha will keep the daily register and invite the children; all three of us will take turns on afternoon duty.
- What things we will need: brooms, gloves, garbage bags, two dustbins, a mat, two benches, story books, board games, four potted plants and a small notice board.
- By what time: the clean-up and the collection of materials in the first week of the vacation; the setting up of the corner and the duty rota in the second week.
- When we will complete the task: the whole task will be completed by the end of the second week of the summer vacation, and we will present our report to the class on the first day of the new session.
explanation: This is a group activity in which the IDEAL tool is applied to a real, small problem of the students' own area. The plan shows all five steps of IDEAL together with the four planning questions (who, what, by when, completion).

question: Exercise 1 (Role play): Work in groups of four, each taking one character. It is time to go on study leave. You and your friends are discussing how to plan your studies so that you can revise all the subjects effectively and efficiently and be well prepared for the exams. Discuss your schedule, expressing your preferences of time, place and subject, giving reasons. Continue the dialogue that begins: Tariq: I don't understand why you want to study so early in the morning. I find it very hard to do so. Saira: One reason is that I'm quite used to waking up early for school as it is... Adnan: Yes, that's the time the mind is fresh after a good night's sleep. What about you, Zohair? Zohair: Well, I ...
answer:
A model continuation of the dialogue:

Zohair: Well, I am afraid I cannot agree with Saira. I prefer studying at night, because the house is quiet then and nobody disturbs me. However, since you all want to start early, I am ready to try the morning routine for one week and see how it works.

Tariq: That is fair enough. As for me, I would rather revise in the afternoon, after a short rest, because I feel sleepy early in the morning. But I do agree that we should all sit together for group study at least three times a week.

Saira: I am glad you agree, Tariq. Now, which subject shall we revise first? I think we should begin with Mathematics, because it needs a fresh mind and daily practice; in my opinion it is the most difficult subject.

Adnan: I am not sure about that. I would prefer to start with English, because it needs more time for reading and writing, and we can do Mathematics later with the help of our group. What do you think, Zohair?

Zohair: I agree with Adnan that English should come first, as we can improve it only by reading and writing every day. But I would suggest that we keep the last hour of every evening for Mathematics practice.

Tariq: That sounds sensible. Where shall we study? I like studying in my own room because there is no noise there.

Saira: I prefer the school library, because it has reference books and there are no distractions. I think we should study there in the mornings and at home in the evenings.

Adnan: I am happy with that plan. Then let us fix our timetable: morning study of English from six to eight at home or in the library, evening group study of Mathematics from five to six, and the remaining subjects on alternate days. We shall meet on Sunday to make the final timetable.

Zohair: I am quite satisfied with this schedule. Let us also agree, politely, that if any of us disagrees later, he will give his reasons with respect, as we have done today.
explanation: This speaking exercise practises asking for and expressing preferences and giving reasons. The model dialogue uses a variety of polite structures such as 'I prefer', 'I would rather', 'I think we should', 'in my opinion' and 'I am afraid I cannot agree', and it ends with an agreed schedule.

question: Exercise 1 Q1: Rewrite the sentence by replacing the bold synonym 'miniature' with an appropriate synonym from the options: He is a brilliant carpenter. He has made a doll house with miniature furniture for every room.
answer: He is a brilliant carpenter. He has made a doll house with tiny furniture for every room.
explanation: 'Miniature' means very small in size, so 'tiny' is the correct synonym here. 'Pretty', 'fresh' and 'tall' do not carry the meaning of smallness.

question: Exercise 1 Q2: Rewrite the sentence by replacing the bold synonym 'difficult' with an appropriate synonym from the options: Mrs Amjad gave the class a difficult assignment for chemistry.
answer: Mrs Amjad gave the class a hard assignment for chemistry.
explanation: 'Difficult' means not easy to do, and 'hard' is its direct synonym. 'Free', 'easy' and 'caring' have quite different meanings.

question: Exercise 1 Q3: Rewrite the sentence by replacing the bold synonym 'old' with an appropriate synonym from the options: My grandmother is old. She is about 90 years old.
answer: My grandmother is elderly. She is about 90 years old.
explanation: 'Elderly' is the polite synonym for 'old' when speaking of a person's age. 'Crazy', 'charming' and 'friendly' describe character, not age.

question: Exercise 1 Q4: Rewrite the sentence by replacing the bold synonym 'slim' with an appropriate synonym from the options: Our principal is very smart and slim.
answer: Our principal is very smart and thin.
explanation: 'Slim' means thin in an attractive way, so 'thin' is the closest synonym here. 'Tall', 'charming' and 'strict' do not mean slim.

question: Exercise 1 Q5: Rewrite the sentence by replacing the bold synonym 'stable' with an appropriate synonym from the options: A stable government ensures that a nation will progress.
answer: A steady government ensures that a nation will progress.
explanation: 'Stable' means firm and not likely to change, so 'steady' is the best synonym. 'Friendly', 'strong' and 'outgoing' do not carry the idea of firmness and continuity.

question: Exercise 1 Q6: Rewrite the sentence by replacing the bold synonym 'help' with an appropriate synonym from the options: Farzana is always ready to help the people in her neighbourhood.
answer: Farzana is always ready to assist the people in her neighbourhood.
explanation: 'Assist' is the formal synonym of 'help'. 'Teach', 'guide' and 'train' mean something more specific than helping.

question: Exercise 1 Q7: Rewrite the sentence by replacing the bold synonym 'drowsy' with an appropriate synonym from the options: I feel drowsy after having rice for lunch.
answer: I feel sleepy after having rice for lunch.
explanation: 'Drowsy' means half asleep, so 'sleepy' is its exact synonym. 'Lazy', 'active' and 'happy' do not mean drowsy.

question: Exercise 1 Q8: Rewrite the sentence by replacing the bold synonym 'vacant' with an appropriate synonym from the options: The house next door has been vacant for two years.
answer: The house next door has been empty for two years.
explanation: 'Vacant' means not occupied or empty, so 'empty' is the correct synonym. 'Dirty', 'robbed' and 'painted' do not give the meaning of vacancy.

question: Exercise 2 (a): Select the most appropriate synonym to complete the sentence: This cup of tea tastes like tea flavoured water. It is very ______ (weak, frail, fragile).
answer: This cup of tea tastes like tea flavoured water. It is very weak.
explanation: 'Weak' is used for drinks that have too little flavour or strength. 'Frail' and 'fragile' are used for people or things that break easily, not for tea.

question: Exercise 2 (b): Select the most appropriate synonym to complete the sentence: If one wants to succeed in the exams, it is ______ to study regularly (primary, important, significant).
answer: If one wants to succeed in the exams, it is important to study regularly.
explanation: 'Important' is the natural word for something necessary to achieve a result. 'Primary' means first in order, and 'significant' means notable, so neither fits this sentence as well.

question: Exercise 2 (c): Select the most appropriate synonym to complete the sentence: During the monsoon rains the water in the rivers becomes very ______ (disordered, violent, rough).
answer: During the monsoon rains the water in the rivers becomes very rough.
explanation: 'Rough' is the word used for disturbed, uneven water. 'Violent' is used for people or acts of force, and 'disordered' is used for things that are not arranged properly.

question: Exercise 2 (d): Select the most appropriate synonym to complete the sentence: The ruins of Moen-jo-Daro are ______ (old, past, aged).
answer: The ruins of Moen-jo-Daro are old.
explanation: 'Old' is the correct word for things that have existed for a long time. 'Past' means gone by in time, and 'aged' is generally used for people or things that have grown grey with years.

question: Exercise 2 (e): Select the most appropriate synonym to complete the sentence: Pakistan is ______ in minerals (rich, wealthy, affluent).
answer: Pakistan is rich in minerals.
explanation: 'Rich in' is the fixed expression used for countries that have plenty of a natural resource. 'Wealthy' and 'affluent' are used for people who have a lot of money.

question: Exercise 2 (f): Select the most appropriate synonym to complete the sentence: My mother has to go to the NADRA office because her ID card is no longer ______ (valid, authorized, legitimate).
answer: My mother has to go to the NADRA office because her ID card is no longer valid.
explanation: 'Valid' means legally usable and still in force, which is exactly the meaning needed for a document such as an identity card.

question: Exercise 2 (g): Select the most appropriate synonym to complete the sentence: The bangles her grandmother gave her are made of ______ gold (true, correct, real).
answer: The bangles her grandmother gave her are made of real gold.
explanation: 'Real' means genuine, not imitation, so it is the right word for pure gold. 'True' means correct or faithful, and 'correct' means free from error; neither is used for metals.

question: Exercise 2 (h): Select the most appropriate synonym to complete the sentence: The teacher asked the students to remain ______ as the class next door was doing a test (still, quiet, noiseless).
answer: The teacher asked the students to remain quiet as the class next door was doing a test.
explanation: 'Quiet' means making little or no noise and is used for people. 'Still' means without movement, and 'noiseless' is generally used for machines or actions, not for people who must keep silent.

question: Exercise 2 (i): Select the most appropriate synonym to complete the sentence: This perfume has a lovely ______ (odour, smell, fragrance).
answer: This perfume has a lovely fragrance.
explanation: 'Fragrance' is the pleasant, sweet smell of a perfume. 'Odour' is often used for an unpleasant smell, and 'smell' is a neutral word.

question: Exercise 2 (j): Select the most appropriate synonym to complete the sentence: The entire staff in the office was full of ______ for the new manager (appreciation, admiration, praise).
answer: The entire staff in the office was full of admiration for the new manager.
explanation: 'Full of admiration for' is the natural collocation, meaning a feeling of great respect and liking. 'Appreciation' and 'praise' are things that are expressed, not feelings one is 'full of'.

question: Exercise 3 (a): Four of the following five words are synonyms; circle the word that is different: friendly, agreeable, pleasant, decent, amicable.
answer: The different word is 'decent'. The other four - friendly, agreeable, pleasant and amicable - all mean kind and easy to get along with.
explanation: 'Decent' means proper, acceptable or respectable; it does not mean friendly, so it does not belong to the group.

question: Exercise 3 (b): Four of the following five words are synonyms; circle the word that is different: option, nice, choice, possibility, alternative.
answer: The different word is 'nice'. The other four - option, choice, possibility and alternative - all mean something that may be chosen or may happen.
explanation: 'Nice' means pleasant or agreeable and has nothing to do with choosing, so it is the odd word out.

question: Exercise 3 (c): Four of the following five words are synonyms; circle the word that is different: reasonable, rude, impolite, cheeky, disrespectful.
answer: The different word is 'reasonable'. The other four - rude, impolite, cheeky and disrespectful - all describe bad manners.
explanation: 'Reasonable' means sensible and fair, which is the opposite of the rudeness shown by the other four words.

question: Exercise 3 (d): Four of the following five words are synonyms; circle the word that is different: severe, serious, harsh, stable, stern.
answer: The different word is 'stable'. The other four - severe, serious, harsh and stern - all mean strict or harsh in nature.
explanation: 'Stable' means firm and not likely to change, which is a different idea from the strictness expressed by the other four words.

question: Exercise 3 (e): Four of the following five words are synonyms; circle the word that is different: huge, large, enormous, mammoth, many.
answer: The different word is 'many'. The other four - huge, large, enormous and mammoth - all mean very big in size.
explanation: 'Many' tells us the number of things, not their size, so it does not belong with the other four words.

question: Exercise 3 (f): Four of the following five words are synonyms; circle the word that is different: rubbish, garbage, garden, trash, refuse.
answer: The different word is 'garden'. The other four - rubbish, garbage, trash and refuse - all mean waste material that is thrown away.
explanation: A garden is a piece of ground where flowers and vegetables are grown, so it has nothing to do with waste.

question: Exercise 3 (g): Four of the following five words are synonyms; circle the word that is different: polite, intelligent, smart, clever, bright.
answer: The different word is 'polite'. The other four - intelligent, smart, clever and bright - all describe a person who has a quick and able mind.
explanation: 'Polite' describes good manners, not intelligence, so it is the odd word in this group.

question: Exercise 3 (h): Four of the following five words are synonyms; circle the word that is different: position, vacancy, opening, clean, post.
answer: The different word is 'clean'. The other four - position, vacancy, opening and post - all mean a job that is available.
explanation: 'Clean' means free from dirt and is an adjective, whereas the other four words are nouns meaning a place of work or an available job.

question: Exercise 3 (i): Four of the following five words are synonyms; circle the word that is different: mistake, correct, error, inaccuracy, slip.
answer: The different word is 'correct'. The other four - mistake, error, inaccuracy and slip - all mean something that is wrong.
explanation: 'Correct' means free from error, which is the opposite of the other four words; it is therefore the odd word out.

question: Exercise 3 (j): Four of the following five words are synonyms; circle the word that is different: disease, ailment, wound, illness, disorder.
answer: The different word is 'wound'. The other four - disease, ailment, illness and disorder - all mean a sickness or a bad condition of health.
explanation: A wound is an injury to the body caused by a cut, blow or weapon, not an illness, so it is the odd word in this group.

question: Exercise 4: Work with a partner. Select any six groups in Exercise 3. Next, pick two synonyms from each of the selected groups and use both these synonyms in your own sentences. Do this work on a piece of paper, exchange it with another pair for feedback, make changes where necessary, and then write the sentences in your notebooks.
answer:
Model sentences using two synonyms from each of six groups of Exercise 3:

Group (a) - friendly / amicable:
1. Our new neighbour is very friendly and always greets us with a smile.
2. After a long argument, the two brothers reached an amicable settlement.

Group (b) - choice / alternative:
3. You must make your own choice about the subjects you wish to study in Class X.
4. Solar power is an excellent alternative to electricity produced from coal.

Group (d) - severe / stern:
5. The severe heat of June made it very difficult to work outdoors.
6. Our coach gave us a stern look when we arrived late for practice.

Group (e) - huge / enormous:
7. A huge crowd had gathered at the stadium to watch the final match.
8. The blue whale is an enormous creature of the sea.

Group (g) - intelligent / clever:
9. Sara is an intelligent student who answers every question thoughtfully.
10. It was a clever plan that saved our team from defeat.

Group (j) - illness / ailment:
11. He stayed at home for a whole week because of a serious illness.
12. Old age often brings minor ailments such as joint pain and poor eyesight.
explanation: This exercise makes the students use synonyms actively rather than only recognising them. Writing the two words in different sentences shows that although they are similar in meaning they are not always interchangeable in a given context.

question: Exercise 5 blank 1: My father is a remarkable man. He has been working ______ he was 15 years old.
answer: My father is a remarkable man. He has been working since he was 15 years old.
explanation: 'Since' is used with a point of time in the past (when he was 15) from which an action has continued up to now, and with the present perfect continuous tense.

question: Exercise 5 blank 2: He has been working ______ he was at school.
answer: He has been working since he was at school.
explanation: Here 'he was at school' is a point of time in the past, so 'since' is needed, not 'for', which would require a period of time.

question: Exercise 5 blank 3: He used to work ______ four hours every day and on weekends.
answer: He used to work for four hours every day and on weekends.
explanation: 'Four hours' is a period or duration of time, and 'for' is used with periods of time in any tense.

question: Exercise 5 blank 4: He has now worked in the same factory ______ 25 years.
answer: He has now worked in the same factory for 25 years.
explanation: '25 years' is the length or duration of the period, so 'for' is used even with the present perfect tense.

question: Exercise 5 blank 5: ______ he started working at the factory, he has been promoted many times.
answer: Since he started working at the factory, he has been promoted many times.
explanation: 'Since' introduces the starting point of an action that continues up to the present; it is placed at the beginning of the clause here and is written with a capital letter.

question: Exercise 5 blank 6: He was initially hired ______ a period of three months.
answer: He was initially hired for a period of three months.
explanation: 'A period of three months' is a duration, so 'for' is the correct preposition.

question: Exercise 5 blank 7: But he has been working there ever ______.
answer: But he has been working there ever since.
explanation: 'Ever since' is a fixed expression meaning continuously from the time mentioned (the end of those first three months) up to now.

question: Exercise 5 blank 8: He started working ______ Rs 25/- a day.
answer: He started working for Rs 25/- a day.
explanation: Here 'for' means 'in exchange for' or 'at a wage of', which is the fixed usage with wages and rates of pay.

question: Exercise 5 blank 9: If he fell ill or if he was absent he did not get paid ______ that day.
answer: If he fell ill or if he was absent he did not get paid for that day.
explanation: 'For that day' means in respect of that particular day; 'for' is used with a period of time even when it is as short as one day.

question: Exercise 5 blank 10: He only took off ______ serious emergencies, like illness and death.
answer: He only took off for serious emergencies, like illness and death.
explanation: 'To take off for something' means to stay away from work because of that reason, so 'for' is used here to show the purpose or cause.

question: Exercise 5 blank 11: In fact, there were periods when he didn't take a single holiday ______ many months at a time.
answer: In fact, there were periods when he didn't take a single holiday for many months at a time.
explanation: 'Many months at a time' is a duration, so 'for' is the correct preposition.

question: Exercise 5 blank 12: He soon earned the respect of his co-workers and boss, and ______ then, he has risen higher and higher.
answer: He soon earned the respect of his co-workers and boss, and since then, he has risen higher and higher.
explanation: 'Since then' marks the point of time (that time) from which his rise has continued up to the present, and it goes with the present perfect tense.

question: Exercise 5 blank 13: He has now worked for the same factory ______ 25 years.
answer: He has now worked for the same factory for 25 years.
explanation: '25 years' is the duration of the period of work, so 'for' is required. (The sentence uses 'for the same factory' in the sense of 'worked in the same factory'.)

question: Exercise 5 blank 14: He was offered retirement when he completed 25 years, but he said that he would like to work ______ a few more years.
answer: He was offered retirement when he completed 25 years, but he said that he would like to work for a few more years.
explanation: 'A few more years' is a period of time, so 'for' is the correct preposition. Here 'would like to work for' also means to work in exchange for those years.

question: Exercise 6: Write a paragraph explaining what your three favourite hobbies or free time activities are or were. Explain why you started, how long you have done them for, when you started them, do you still do them, and why you like them so much. Remember to use 'for' and 'since' in your sentences.
answer:
Model paragraph:

One thing I like doing during my free time is reading. I have been reading story books since I was ten years old, when my elder sister gave me a collection of folk tales and I fell in love with stories at once. So I have been reading story books for nearly six years now. Although I have been reading since I was ten, I think I will do it for many more years; in fact, I think I will do it for the rest of my life. Another thing I enjoy is playing cricket with my friends in the street. I started playing it when I was in Class VI, because our physical training teacher told us that games keep the body healthy and the mind fresh. I have been playing cricket for about three years now, and I still play every evening whenever my school work is finished. Yet another thing that I did for a long time was gardening with my grandfather. I began helping him in our small garden when I was eight, and we worked together for almost four years. Sadly, my grandfather passed away two years ago and we moved to a flat, so I have not done any gardening since then; but I still love plants, and I hope to start a small garden of my own one day.
explanation: The exercise practises 'for' (with a duration - for three years, for the rest of my life) and 'since' (with a starting point - since I was ten, since then). The model paragraph answers all the questions asked: what, why, how long, when, whether it continues, and why the writer likes the activity.

question: Exercise 1 (Narrative Essay - Further Practice): Imagine you are reporters for a newspaper. An important event has taken place in your area and you have to write a report and submit it for publication. Work in groups of three, share one important event or incident each, choose one of the stories and, following the steps given in Unit 2.4 Exercise 3, write a narrative essay of at least four paragraphs about it.
answer:
Model narrative report (newspaper style):

A Free Medical Camp Brings Relief to the People of Our Town

By: A Student Reporter, Class IX

Our town, which has more than twenty thousand residents, has only one government dispensary and no proper hospital. For years the poor people of our area had to travel forty kilometres to the city even for a small check-up. Last Sunday, however, an important event took place that brought great relief to hundreds of families: a free medical camp was set up in the Government Boys' School ground by a group of volunteer doctors and the students of our school.

The camp began at eight o'clock in the morning and continued until sunset. Ten doctors and nurses, most of them from the city's teaching hospital, examined the patients free of charge, and medicines were also given free of cost. The volunteers had arranged four separate sections - one for children, one for women, one for eye patients and one for general check-ups. In the afternoon a short talk on cleanliness and the prevention of dengue fever was also given to the waiting crowd. I myself helped at the registration desk, where more than six hundred patients were registered during the day.

The event had been organised after a sad incident that had shaken our town only a month earlier. A nine-year-old boy of our neighbourhood, the son of a poor cart-puller, had died of typhoid because his father could not afford to take him to the city for treatment. His death made the students of our school realise that good health is the right of every human being and not a luxury of the rich. The students collected donations, the local traders gave medicines, and the school management allowed the use of the ground. The camp cost almost nothing to the poor patients because everybody contributed according to his ability.

The significance of this event is very great, both for my town and for me personally. For the town it means that hundreds of people received treatment and advice who would otherwise have remained ill, and it has taught our people that we can solve our own problems by working together. For me personally, it was a lesson in service and social responsibility. I learnt that a report is not merely a description of an event; it is a record of what a community can achieve when its members join hands.
explanation: A narrative report tells when and where the event took place, what happened with significant details, and why it matters at the personal, social and national levels. This model follows the structure taught in Unit 2.4 - introduction setting the scene, the event itself, the circumstances that led to it, and a concluding paragraph on its importance.

question: Exercise 2 (Summary Writing): Work in pairs. Read the passage 'Helen Keller' and underline the main ideas/words in each paragraph; do not include any details. The first paragraph has been done as an example.
answer:
Main ideas/key words of each paragraph of the passage 'Helen Keller':

Paragraph 1 (the example): Most people are lucky to be able to see and hear, but some people are blind and deaf; those who lost their sight and hearing after once having them are the most unfortunate; many such people are brave and courageous - and one of them was Helen Keller.

Paragraph 2: Helen Keller was born in 1880 in a small town in the United States of America; she was a normal child up to the age of two; in February 1882 she fell seriously ill and became blind and deaf; her parents were sad but never lost hope.

Paragraph 3: When Helen was seven her life changed completely; her father heard about Miss Sullivan, a woman who had once been blind but had regained her sight and who now helped blind people; her father asked Miss Sullivan to come and teach Helen, and she agreed.

Paragraph 4: One day at the river bank Miss Sullivan taught Helen to spell 'water' by dipping her hand in the water; Helen felt excited because there was now some light in her dark world; kindly and patiently Miss Sullivan went on to teach her about mountains, rivers, history, geography, counting and sums.

Paragraph 5: When Helen was eight she was sent to a school for blind children; although she could speak she had forgotten how, so her teacher helped her to regain her speech by making her feel the movements of her lips; after many exercises, at the age of ten, she was able to speak again.

Paragraph 6: By and by Helen learnt to read books printed in Braille by touching the raised points with her fingers; she read as much as other people, passed all her examinations easily, went to college and then to Harvard University, and graduated without difficulty, proving to be a better student than many others.

Paragraph 7: In 1956, at seventy-six, Helen Keller visited Pakistan to see how she could help other deaf and blind people; she addressed many gatherings and encouraged those with similar shortcomings, visited the school for the deaf, dumb and blind in Karachi, told the students to be happy and cheerful and never to curse their fate, and praised the volunteers for their zeal and self-less dedication.
explanation: Underlining the main ideas and key words of each paragraph, and leaving out details, is the first step of summary writing. The seven main ideas listed here are the skeleton from which the summary in Exercise 3 is written.

question: Exercise 3: Work in pairs. Use the underlined key words and write a summary of the passage 'Helen Keller'. Look at the Do's and Don'ts given in the boxes in Unit 2.4. You may begin like this: 'Most people are very lucky as they can see all things around them. But some people cannot see or hear...'
answer:
Summary of the passage 'Helen Keller':

Most people are very lucky as they can see all things around them. But some people cannot see or hear. However, there are also those unfortunate ones who could once see and hear but are now blind and deaf. Some such people are brave and they take this as a challenge. One such person was Helen Keller. She was born in America in 1880 and was a normal child up to the age of two, but in February 1882 she fell seriously ill and became blind and deaf. Her parents were sad, yet they never lost hope. When Helen was seven, her life changed completely, because Miss Sullivan, a woman who had once been blind but had regained her sight, came to teach her. Miss Sullivan first taught her the word 'water' by dipping her hand in the river, and then patiently taught her about mountains and rivers, history and geography, counting and sums. When Helen was eight she was sent to a school for blind children, where her teacher helped her to regain her lost speech by letting her feel the movements of her lips; by the age of ten she could speak again. She learnt to read books printed in Braille by touching the raised points with her fingers, passed all her examinations easily, went to college and then to Harvard University, and graduated without difficulty. In 1956, although she was seventy-six, she visited Pakistan to help the deaf and blind. She encouraged them to be happy and cheerful and told them that they could do everything in this world.
explanation: A good summary keeps only the main ideas, follows the order of the original, uses the writer's own words where possible, does not repeat details or examples, and gives the whole passage in about one-fourth of its length. This model of about 250 words fits all these rules.

question: Exercise 1: Work in pairs. Read the information about K2 given in the table and write an essay about K2 by following these steps: (1) Discuss in how many paragraphs you can divide the given information. (2) Write an introductory paragraph about Pakistan, its physical features and the high mountains of Northern Pakistan, ending with a sentence stating what you will write about K2. (3) Write a good topic sentence for each paragraph. (4) Write the supporting details for each topic sentence (3-5 sentences). (5) Write a concluding paragraph. (6) Edit for spelling, punctuation and grammar. (7) Exchange your essay with another pair and give feedback. (8) Revise and write it in your notebooks.
answer:
Plan: The information in the table divides naturally into five paragraphs - (i) introduction on Pakistan and its mountains, (ii) location, height and range of K2, (iii) the names and nicknames of K2, (iv) the history of its climbing, and (v) Pakistani climbers, danger and conclusion.

K2: The Savage Mountain of Pakistan

Pakistan is a land of striking physical beauty. It has high mountains, green valleys, glaciers, rivers, lakes and deserts, and among all these features the mountains of the north are the most impressive. These areas are the meeting place of the three greatest mountain ranges in the world - the Himalayas, the Karakoram and the Hindu Kush - and they contain some of the highest peaks on the earth. This essay describes one of those peaks, K2, the mightiest mountain of Pakistan.

K2 is the second-highest mountain in the world and the highest mountain of Pakistan. It stands on the Pakistan-China border, between Gilgit in Gilgit-Baltistan and the Tashkurgan Tajik Autonomous County of Xinjiang in China, and it forms part of the Karakoram range. Its height is 28,253 feet, that is 8,612 metres, which makes it the second-highest peak in the world after Mount Everest and the highest peak within Pakistan.

The mountain has several names. The name 'K2' was given in 1852 by the British surveyor T. G. Montgomerie: 'K' stands for the Karakoram range and '2' for the second-highest peak. It was later named Mount Godwin-Austen after Haversham Godwin-Austen, a British surveyor and explorer. The local Balti people call it Chogori, meaning 'large mountain'; in Chinese it is Qogir, meaning 'Great Mountain'; and another local name is Kechu. Because of its terrible weather and high death rate it is nicknamed the 'Savage Mountain'.

K2 is also one of the hardest mountains in the world to climb. The first attempt to reach its summit was made in 1902 by the British climbers Aleister Crowley and Oscar Eckenstein, who reached 18,600 feet (5,670 metres). The summit was first reached on 31 July 1954 by the Italians Achille Compagnoni and Lino Lacedelli. The usual season for climbing is June, July or August, and for a long time K2 had never been climbed in winter; the first successful winter climb was completed on 26 February 2016 by Ali Sadpara of Pakistan, Alex Txikon and Simone Moro.

Pakistanis are justly proud of their own climbers on K2. Ashraf Aman became the first Pakistani to reach the summit on 9 August 1977, and on 26 July 2014 the first team of Pakistani climbers reached K2. The mountain is, however, extremely dangerous: till 2014, over 335 climbers had reached the summit while at least 82 people had died, giving a death rate of about 27 per cent. K2, therefore, is the pride of Pakistan - a beautiful but deadly mountain that has tested the courage of the world's best climbers for more than a century and has made the name of our country famous all over the world.
explanation: This Study Skills exercise teaches the students to convert points into a connected essay. The model shows the paragraph plan, a general introduction about Pakistan that narrows down to K2, clear topic sentences, supporting details of three to five sentences in each paragraph, and a concluding paragraph that sums up the significance of the mountain.

question: Exercise 2: Work individually and write an essay on Nanga Parbat, following the same steps as in Exercise 1. After you have completed, exchange your work with your partner, give each other feedback, revise your essay and write it in your notebook.
answer:
Plan: The table information on Nanga Parbat divides into five paragraphs - (i) introduction on Pakistan and its northern mountains, (ii) location, height and range, (iii) the name and its meaning, (iv) climbing history and records, and (v) the danger and the conclusion.

Nanga Parbat: The Killer Mountain

Pakistan is a country of wonderful natural beauty, and its northern areas are famous all over the world for their lofty mountains, glaciers and green valleys. Among the giant peaks of the north, one of the most famous is Nanga Parbat, which stands like a white wall at the western end of the Himalayas. This essay presents the main facts about this great mountain.

Nanga Parbat is the ninth-highest mountain in the world and the second-highest mountain in Pakistan. It lies in the Northern Areas of Pakistan, between Chilas and Astore, in the district of Diamer, and it belongs to the Himalayan range. Its height is 8,126 metres, that is 26,660 feet, which makes it one of the highest mountains on the earth.

The mountain is known by several names. 'Nanga Parbat' literally means 'Naked Mountain', perhaps because its rocky summit is often swept bare of snow by fierce winds. Its local name is Diamer or Deo Mir, which means 'huge mountain'. These beautiful names hide, however, a very dangerous reality, for the mountain has earned a terrible nickname as well.

Nanga Parbat is called the 'Killer Mountain', and with good reason. The first attempt to climb it was made in 1895 by Albert F. Mummery and his team, who reached almost 6,100 metres (20,000 feet) but never returned. In all, 31 people died trying to climb the mountain before its first ascent. The summit was first reached on 3 July 1953 by the Austrian climber Hermann Buhl, in one of the greatest feats in the history of mountaineering. The mountain has since been climbed in both summer and winter; the first successful winter climb was made on 26 February 2016 by Ali Sadpara of Pakistan, Alex Txikon and Simone Moro. Even so, the mountain has taken a heavy toll: till 2012, at least 68 climbers had died on it, giving a death rate of 22.3 per cent.

Nanga Parbat, therefore, is both a wonder and a warning. It shows the immense beauty and the immense power of nature at the same time. The courage and sacrifice of the climbers who have attempted it, and especially of our own Pakistani mountaineers such as Ali Sadpara, have won honour for Pakistan and inspired thousands of young people to face difficulties with patience and daring.
explanation: This exercise repeats the article-from-points skill of Exercise 1 with a new set of points about Nanga Parbat. The model again shows a paragraph plan, an introduction that moves from the general to the particular, topic sentences, supporting details and a conclusion.

question: Doing Something Different: Think of one thing that you would like to do when you grow up; think of doing something different, something that people do not normally do. State what you will do, why you want to do it, and how you will do it. Then take a piece of paper and show what you will do, why you will do it and how, using writing, drawings or pictures and colours. Make your presentation bright and colourful. Afterwards, share your dream with the rest of the class by showing them your paper presentation.
answer:
Model response (with a note of what to draw on the paper):

What I will do: When I grow up, I want to become a maker of musical instruments from waste materials - an 'eco-musician'. I would like to open a small workshop where broken buckets, old tins, bamboo, bottle tops and dry gourds are turned into drums, flutes, guitars and rattles for children.

Why I want to do it: I want to do this because it is something that people do not normally do. Most people throw away waste and buy new things, but I want to show that beautiful music can be created out of things that others call rubbish. In this way I can give poor children free musical instruments, keep our streets cleaner and reduce the harm that plastic waste does to our environment. Music also brings joy to people, and I want to spread that joy.

How I will do it: First, I will learn how musical instruments are made by watching video lessons and by requesting a local carpenter and a tabla maker to teach me in the holidays. Then I will collect waste material from shops and homes through a school campaign. In my workshop I will clean the material, cut and polish it safely, and fit strings, skins and pipes to make simple instruments. Finally, I will give these instruments to children and teach them in free weekly classes. In this way, waste will become music.

What to show on the paper: Divide the chart into three parts and label them 'WHAT', 'WHY' and 'HOW'.
- WHAT: draw a bright picture of my workshop with a guitar made from a tin, a drum from an old bucket and a flute from bamboo.
- WHY: write the three reasons - to make good use of waste, to reduce pollution and to bring free music to poor children.
- HOW: draw four small pictures showing the four steps - collecting waste, learning from elders, building the instruments and teaching the children. Use colour pencils and large clear headings so that the presentation looks bright and attractive.
explanation: The Fun section is not formally assessed; its aim is to let the students enjoy the language while thinking out of the box. This model supplies the three required points (what, why, how) and also a concrete plan for the coloured paper presentation that the students must show to the class.
